preamble: A glottal stop [ʔ] is inserted to give a vowel-initial syllable an onset or to break up vowel hiatus. Dutch inserts it between vowels in hiatus, as in beamen [bəˈʔaːmə(n)]. Bohemian Czech uses it at word and morpheme boundaries before a vowel. Malay and Indonesian insert it where a vowel-final prefix or stem meets a vowel. The inserted stop is predictable and usually not written.

examples.note: [ʔ] separates /ə/ or /aː/ from a following vowel; it also occurs in compounds such as mee-eten and hippie-ideaal.
Glottal stops are most common in compounds where both elements have the same vowel at the boundary (hippie-ideaal, kilo-ohm).
Inserted at a morpheme boundary before a vowel; usual in Bohemia, while Moravian speakers say [znɛuʒiːvat].
Inserted at a word boundary between two vowels; also trojúhelník [trojʔuːɦɛlɲiːk] 'triangle'.

languageExamples.context: Before a vowel at word and morpheme boundaries, mainly in Bohemia

examples.note: A glottal stop is inserted to avoid vowel hiatus at the prefix-stem boundary and is not written.
Inserted when a stem ending in /a/ takes the suffix -an; likewise bacaan [ba.t͡ʃa.ʔan] 'reading'.

languageExamples.context: Between vowels at an affix boundary

examples.note: The prothetic glottal stop stayed after the initial vowel was lost, contrasting with *mune > /ɴni/ 'chest'.
Contrasts with /wa/ 'I'; Amami Ōshima underwent the same glottal-stop epenthesis before vowel-initial words.
